Before trying to improve the yield number, I separated inspection errors from actual process defects so that equipment and process actions targeted the right cause. Production stabilization result Period / basis During tenure at Kumyang · May 2024–Sep 2025 Project form Company project · Assembly process lead Problem to solve Effective good yield was initially about 40%, while production, quality, and equipment teams were using different denominators and defect definitions.
My scope Aligned production, inspection, retest, scrap, and defect definitions, then coordinated improvement schedules and retest results.Used MSA results to separate judgement errors from real defects, then checked jig tolerance, recipe, consumables, vision, and inspection conditions one factor at a time. Verified result / current stage Measured result · Team Effective good yield in the reviewed scope: about 40%→98.7% Verified output · Individual Reflected confirmed conditions in SOP, QCP, P-FMEA, inspection criteria, and training material Team boundary Yield was a cross-functional team result. My role as assembly process lead was to align criteria, priorities, and revalidation.
Disclosure scope: Company source data and customer specifications are confidential, so this case is anonymized and limited to career records and work I directly performed.
The sequence below generalizes the actual work within a publicly shareable scope.
The three-minute case Why it mattered Good-product yield on the 2170 assembly line was initially about 40%. Changing equipment conditions from that headline number alone could mistake a judgment error for a real defect. The reverse was equally risky: treating an actual process defect as an inspection issue would allow it to recur. Before changing the process, the production, inspection, retest, and scrap quantities needed one yield denominator.
My scope As the assembly-process lead, I organized the production plan, WIP, defects, and downtime. I aligned the denominator and defect names used by production, quality, equipment, and development, coordinated the MSA review and condition-by-condition retests, and carried confirmed conditions into field standards.
Workflow Align the yield denominator → separate judgment error from actual defects with MSA → check jigs, recipes, consumables, and inspection conditions → retest one condition at a time → update SOP, QCP, and P-FMEA
Key decisions and verification I used MSA to review operator judgment error and measurement-system variation before classifying actual process defects. Jigs, recipes, consumable wear, and inspection conditions were checked as one system, but only one condition changed in each trial. The test item, inspection method, and decision rule stayed fixed. A condition entered the line baseline only after repeat results supported it. Result and standardization The team result recorded in career material was an improvement in good-product yield from about 40% to 98.7%. Confirmed conditions and checks were added to SOPs, QCP, P-FMEA, inspection criteria, and operator training. The practical standard was that different operators and shifts would calculate and judge yield on the same basis.
Transferability When yield is low, verify the denominator and the measurement system before tuning a recipe. Then separate equipment, consumable, and inspection variables and retest one condition at a time so the cause and effect remain explainable.
Limits The 98.7% figure is a career result for this line, verification period, and denominator, not a public-data recalculation or a universal result for every 2170 line. Company drawings, recipes, raw quality records, and customer specifications remain confidential.

Useful learning requires more than showing many questions: answers must remain hidden before submission, and evidence must explain why an answer is right or wrong afterward. My scope Designed and validated the select→submit→evidence→mistake-review flow, publication decisions, and answer non-disclosure before submission. The case follows the learner's actual path from question selection through mistake review.
Problem Maintenance-qualification material fragments questions, answers, theory, NCS units, and practical visuals across sources. A fluent AI explanation can still teach the wrong thing when answer candidates conflict or image rights are unclear. A learning flow also fails if the answer or explanation is already present in the client response before submission, even when the screen hides it.
The project did not start with a question-volume target. It publishes only material with verified answer, source, and rights evidence. Anything missing one of those elements keeps the same ID and an explicit reason while staying out of the public set.
Representative user scene A learner selects a CBT question, chooses an answer, and submits it. Before submission, the learner receives no answer, explanation, or option-level feedback. After submission, the learner sees the answer and explanation together with the linked source and theory evidence. A wrong option becomes a path back through that evidence for mistake-based learning.
Written-response and practical material follow the same evidence rules without being forced into one answer format. A question or visual without sufficient publication support stays out of the learning path with its deferral reason preserved.
What the tool does—and does not do The tool connects question selection, submission, evidence review, and mistake learning. Each question carries a stable ID, assessment type, answer state, theory link, source, rights state, publication decision, and deferral reason. Publication eligibility means the answer, source, and rights have all been checked; it does not merely mean that content exists.
The tool does not replace official exam material or guarantee a passing outcome. It does not publish an explanation merely because AI finds it plausible. Answer conflicts remain held_answer_conflict; missing visual evidence or unclear rights remain held_asset_missing.
Data, AI, and human roles The data keeps evidence and review state beside the question. Question, theory, NCS evidence, answer state, rights, and publication status share a stable identity so later evidence can be added without erasing the history of uncertainty.
AI assisted with classification, duplicate and semantic-mismatch candidates, explanation and option-feedback drafts, and regression-check ideas. A human reviewed original sources, actual answers, conflicts, image and drawing rights, publication decisions, and final deployment approval. AI plausibility is not publication evidence.
Build sequence Inventory source material and reviewed notes, then assign stable IDs. Separate CBT, written-response, and practical types and connect questions to theory, NCS evidence, and sources. Review answer conflicts and visual rights, keeping incomplete material out of publication. Use Next.js App Router, TypeScript, Zod, and Tailwind to build the select→submit→evidence→mistake-learning flow. Equipment acceptance is not complete when a machine merely runs; product tolerance, repeatability, safety, and production readiness must be checked against shared criteria. Equipment acceptance and initial production stabilization Period / basis During the relevant employment · May 2023–May 2024 Project form Company project · Pilot-line commissioning and operation Problem to solve Thirteen processes and eleven key machines required aligned acceptance criteria, supplier actions, retest records, and a daily 200-cell production plan.
My scope Prepared acceptance sheets, in-process tolerances, and inspection criteria, then tracked FAT/SAT findings and punch-list closure.Managed material, WIP, operators, and lot history for a 200-cell daily plan, using Excel VBA tracking where MES functions were not yet available. Yield and delivery were team results.
Disclosure scope: Equipment drawings, customer specifications, and raw measurements remain confidential; only the verified acceptance process and my scope are described.
The sequence below generalizes the actual work within a publicly shareable scope.
The three-minute case Why it mattered An automatic cycle on one machine does not make a pilot line production-ready. Interfaces and acceptance criteria must work across the line, and unmet items must be retested against the same criteria after supplier action. The task was to manage 13 detailed processes and 11 core systems as one acceptance flow.
My scope My scope covered acceptance criteria and FAT/SAT sheets, Punch List tracking, supplier actions and retest review, and daily 200-cell production operation. I connected equipment action status with material, WIP, and work priorities. Yield and delivery metrics are identified separately as team results.
Workflow Define acceptance criteria → FAT/SAT → Punch List → supplier action → retest → daily 200-cell operation
Key decisions and verification Acceptance criteria were defined before testing so the supplier and site team judged the same items. A Punch List item was not closed on a planned action alone. I tracked the supplier action through a retest against the same criterion. Production planning did not sit outside equipment acceptance. The daily 200-cell operation checked whether material, WIP, and work flow held together after FAT/SAT. Result and standardization The team recorded at least 95% pilot assembly yield and 100% delivery compliance. Acceptance criteria, Punch List and retest results, work standards, and production-history rules were connected so equipment acceptance led into daily operation on one baseline.
Transferability Equipment acceptance is not a one-time FAT or SAT event. A line is ready only when acceptance criteria, open items, supplier actions, retests, and actual production operation remain traceable as one chain.
Limits The yield and delivery figures are team results from pilot production, not long-term mass-production performance or a claim about each machine in isolation. Company acceptance records, equipment drawings, recipes, and customer specifications remain confidential.

30-second summary
A platform that selects domain knowledge and rules from an ontology and LLM wiki to compose and run AI agents with defined roles, tools, evidence, and stop conditions. Authority and evidence checks form its execution-safety layer. Agent composition and local execution foundation verified · not connected to production Period / basis Last completed local validation snapshot · Jul 2026 Project form Personal AI use · Ontology- and LLM-wiki-based agent platform Problem to solve Repeating knowledge, tools, and rules in every long prompt creates inconsistent terminology and opaque agent definitions. Mixing in execution authority can also lead to an unapproved external change.
My scope Designed the flow that selects relevant ontology and LLM-wiki knowledge, composes agent roles, tools, evidence, outputs, and stop conditions, and checks approval and result read-back around external changes. Verified result / current stage Verified output · Individual AI agent composition and execution platform that binds roles, tools, evidence, and stop conditions to ontology and LLM-wiki knowledge Current stage · Individual Agent composition, local execution foundation, and safety layer verified · not connected to production Team boundary AI assists request classification, knowledge retrieval, agent-definition drafts, and result summaries. People decide knowledge standards, tool boundaries, and approval for external changes.
Disclosure scope: The public case covers agent composition, local execution, and the last completed safety-layer validation; internal ontology/wiki content, repositories, environments, and authority details remain private.
The article generalizes how ontology and wiki knowledge is selected to compose and run an agent through a practical work example.
What this platform is Approval gates are not the product by themselves. This project is an AI agent platform that uses knowledge, terminology, and operating rules from an ontology and an LLM wiki to compose and run an agent for a requested task.
The ontology connects related concepts such as equipment, processes, documents, and roles. The LLM wiki provides task guidance, operating sequences, tool instructions, and cautions. The platform selects the relevant knowledge and assembles an executable agent definition containing its role, tools, evidence sources, output format, and stop conditions.
Authority, approval, and evidence checks are the platform’s safety layer. The ability to generate an answer does not automatically permit an agent to submit an order, deploy a change, or modify access. Evidence and human approval are checked separately before an external effect is allowed.
Why I built it When an agent is defined only through a long prompt, terminology can be interpreted inconsistently and the same rules must be repeated for every project. Source documents and tool boundaries also become mixed into the conversation. As the number of agents grows, knowledge and operating rules are duplicated, and a correction may reach only some agents.
I separated reusable knowledge into the ontology and wiki, then selected only the parts needed for each execution. The goal was to make an agent’s knowledge and action boundary inspectable outside its prompt and let several agents share the same knowledge contract.
Representative user scene Consider a request to identify likely causes of repeated equipment stops and propose an inspection sequence.
Classify the equipment, symptom, related process, and expected output in the request. Find connected equipment, parts, failure modes, and inspection documents in the ontology. Retrieve the sequence, allowed tools, sources, and restrictions from the LLM wiki. Compose the analysis agent’s role, inputs, tools, output format, and stop conditions. Run the agent within the allowed data and tool boundary while recording its evidence and result. If the task would change an external system, check the human approval scope, allow or stop the action, and read back the actual result after execution. This is a generalized public description of the implemented direction. It excludes company documents, equipment addresses, accounts, and private operating rules.
Components and responsibilities Component Responsibility Ontology Connect domain concepts and relationships so agents resolve the same objects consistently LLM wiki Provide task guidance, tool instructions, examples, constraints, and validation criteria Agent Composer Turn a request into an executable definition of role, tools, evidence, output, and stop conditions Agent Runner Execute the definition within its allowed boundary and record the process and result Authority & Evidence Layer Check evidence, target identity, and human approval; stop when information is missing and read back the result after execution This separation means a knowledge change can be made in the ontology or wiki instead of editing every agent prompt. The runner records which knowledge was used, while the safety layer keeps analytical success separate from execution authority.
Data, AI, and human roles The ontology and wiki retain concepts, relationships, task guidance, sources, scope, and constraints. An agent run records the request, selected knowledge, tools, result, risk, and approval boundary separately. This makes it possible to inspect how an agent was composed and which material it used.
AI assists with request classification, candidate knowledge retrieval, agent-definition drafts, test and counterexample creation, and result summaries. A person reviews the ontology and wiki, chooses the permitted tools and data scope, and approves any external change. A better answer does not transfer human authority to the agent.
Implemented and verified scope In the last completed local snapshot, Python 3.12 and jsonschema were used to validate agent execution definitions, evidence and target bindings, and stop conditions.
150 local regression checks passed Primary and reproduced artifacts rebuilt from source were byte-identical One Windows symlink capability limitation remained recorded as a skip No orders were submitted and no external systems were changed No human operational approval or production connection exists This verifies a local foundation and safety layer for composing and running agents. It does not mean that a public service, live trading, or external-system automation is operational.
Potential company use A company could compose maintenance, process-diagnostic, quality-investigation, or work-standard search agents that use the same internal terms and rules. Knowledge remains in the ontology and wiki, while each agent receives only the role and tools required for its task, reducing duplicated knowledge and prompt variation.
The platform can also retain which knowledge and documents were used, who approved an external change, and what the external system reported afterward. Actual benefit would still need to be measured through company-data integration, user validation, and operating-environment tests.
Limitations and disclosure This remains a locally validated foundation with no public repository or operating URL. Credentials, internal IPs, private repository and Notion addresses, personal data, and in-progress specifications remain private.
Real operation still requires quality review of the company ontology and wiki, document-level access control, bounded agent tools, human approval, duplicate-execution protection, and read-back from the external system. The current result is not presented as production readiness or live-operation performance.

Matching process conditions alone was not enough; bath condition and cross-instrument differences had to be understood so internal and customer measurements agreed. Process and inspection criteria applied to production Period / basis During tenure at YMC · Mar 2016–Jan 2021 Project form Company project · Surface-treatment process development and qualification Problem to solve If anodizing, etching, cleaning, bath analysis, and inspection measurements were not connected, sample results varied and qualification criteria were difficult to align.
My scope Defined surface-treatment and bath-analysis criteria, then checked analytical reliability through repeat measurement and external comparison.Reviewed bias, Gage R&R, and sample results across instruments and prepared technical-audit and qualification material. Verified result / current stage Verified output · Team Process-change qualification approved and applied to production Verified output · Individual Documented recipes, run sheets, process standards, and inspection criteria Team boundary Qualification and production application were joint outcomes across R&D, quality, production, and the customer. My role was to connect process, analysis, inspection, and validation evidence.
Disclosure scope: Customer identity, detailed specifications, recipes, and bath formulations are confidential; only the verified development and validation flow is described.
The sequence below generalizes the actual work within a publicly shareable scope.
The three-minute case Why it mattered Anodizing, etching, and cleaning results depend on both bath condition and the measurement method used to judge the sample. Stable internal readings were not enough if the customer instrument produced a different result on the same sample. The process condition and measurement baseline had to be aligned together.
My scope I reviewed bath analysis and sampling rules and supported sample validation for anodizing, etching, and cleaning. I compared the same samples across internal and customer instruments, confirmed the correlation, and recorded conditions confirmed through customer qualification in recipes, run sheets, and inspection standards.
Workflow Bath analysis → sample validation → internal/customer cross-instrument correlation → customer qualification confirmation → recipe, run sheet, and inspection-standard updates
Key decisions and verification Bath condition, sample preparation, and measurement method were reviewed separately instead of being changed together. The same samples were used across instruments so sample differences did not distort the correlation check. Only conditions confirmed within customer qualification were transferred into standards, with detailed conditions controlled in the recipe and run sheet. Result and standardization Sample validation and cross-instrument correlation established the conditions confirmed through customer qualification. Recipes, run sheets, and inspection standards were updated together so process settings and measurement decisions did not drift apart.
Transferability A surface-treatment standard cannot stop at bath analysis. Cross-instrument comparison on the same sample and the decision method confirmed in customer qualification must connect back to the process documents.
Limits Company analysis records and customer specifications remain confidential. Actual bath formulations, recipe values, and product identifiers are anonymized, and a condition confirmed on one sample is not generalized to every material or geometry.

There is no separate public GitHub repository or report. Qualification and production application are described from career records.

An overhaul process dependent on individual memory had to be documented as work and inspection criteria so different operators could reproduce the same quality. SOP and checklist applied in work Period / basis During tenure at Bontech · Feb 2021–Mar 2022 Project form Company project · Precision-assembly standardization Problem to solve Disassembly and assembly order, torque, alignment, leak, and repeatability checks were largely passed on verbally, creating omission and operator-variation risk.
My scope Performed vacuum-robot disassembly, cleaning, component replacement, precision assembly, arm alignment, encoder zeroing, and commissioning.Documented parts, sequence, torque, inspection points, and abnormal-condition actions in SOPs and checklists used for operator training. Verified result / current stage Measured result · Team Team monthly shipment volume in the same period: 1–2→4–5 units Verified output · Individual Disassembly, assembly, and inspection SOPs, checklists, and operator training material Team boundary Monthly shipment volume was a team result for the same period. My scope was overhaul work, inspection standardization, and training.
Disclosure scope: Customer names, specifications, drawings, and site details are withheld; only my direct assembly, inspection, and standardization work is described.
The sequence below generalizes the actual work within a publicly shareable scope.
The three-minute case Why it mattered Vacuum-robot overhaul depended heavily on verbal instruction and individual experience. Disassembly and assembly order varied by operator, and torque, alignment, leak, and repeatability checks did not always read as one continuous workflow. The practical need was to turn experienced judgment into a baseline another operator could follow.
My scope I performed vacuum-robot disassembly and assembly while organizing the torque, alignment, leak, and repeatability checks. I converted the field sequence and decision items into SOPs and checklists, then used them in operator training and initial work review.
Workflow Review verbal work practices → document disassembly and assembly → connect torque, alignment, leak, and repeatability checks → issue SOPs and checklists → train operators
Key decisions and verification The documents linked each assembly stage to the inspection item and decision sequence that followed it. Torque and alignment were treated as assembly conditions; leak and repeatability were treated as result checks. This made omissions visible. The SOPs and checklists were used in actual work so I could check whether the next operator reproduced the same sequence. Result and standardization Verbal know-how became SOPs, checklists, and training material used on the shop floor. During the same period, team output increased from 1–2 to 4–5 units per month. This was a team result, not my individual output, and I do not attribute the increase to the documents alone.
Transferability An overhaul standard needs more than a disassembly and assembly sequence. Fastening and alignment conditions, leak and repeatability checks, and operator training must sit in one reproducible flow.
Limits The customer remains anonymous, and company drawings, customer specifications, and detailed torque values remain confidential. I do not claim a final customer approval that I did not personally verify.
Links and evidence The public evidence for this case is the de-identified career account and the blueprint below. In an interview I can explain the work sequence, how the checks were connected, and how the documents were used in training.

contents:
30-second summary
For manufacturing data, a repeatable path from preprocessing through evaluation matters more than listing many model names. Learning workflow public · Before manufacturing validation Period / basis Personal learning project · Current public-repository scope Project form Reproducible modeling study repository Problem to solve When preprocessing, split, training, and evaluation conditions are scattered, it is difficult to explain whether performance differences come from the model or data handling.
My scope Organized preprocessing, model training, evaluation, and reproducibility management into one repository workflow. Verified result / current stage Verified output · Individual Public learning flow from preprocessing to training, evaluation, and reproducibility management Current stage · Individual Before application to production data and field-performance validation Team boundary This is a personal learning repository and is not presented as a result from company production data.
Disclosure scope: Only experiment procedures visible in public code are described; unverified performance figures are excluded.
The workflow is generalized as validation needed before applying models to manufacturing data.
Why the shop-floor decision mattered Deep-learning code can run once and still be unusable for an engineering decision if no one can explain which data and settings produced the result. A score can be overstated when samples from the same product or Lot cross training and test boundaries, or when the test set is repeatedly used to guide model changes.
In manufacturing, that problem affects quality decisions directly. Missed defects and false rejections have different costs, and offline behavior can change with equipment, material, or capture conditions. The project therefore starts with a traceable experiment standard rather than a peak score.
Why a digital method was needed A single notebook is useful for fast exploration, but hidden state and cell order can make a result fragile. Separating preprocessing, training, evaluation, and run records makes it possible to trace which change affected the outcome.
MLOps in this case does not mean that a deployment platform has already been built. It means connecting the data identifier, split rule, configuration, code, runtime environment, and evaluation output as one experiment record.
My actual role As a personal learning and practical-validation project, I documented a modeling standard that connects problem definition, data splitting, preprocessing, training, evaluation, and reproducibility. The focus is to establish a simple baseline, compare candidates on the same split and evaluation functions, and read metrics together with error cases.
Because the current public material is limited, this case is a design document rather than a list of completed features. It does not claim a specific dataset size, model accuracy, completed training run, or production deployment.
Data flow Preserve and split source data → preprocessing → configuration-based training → fixed evaluation and error analysis → reproducibility record linking data, code, environment, and results
Preprocessing parameters are fitted only on training data and then applied to validation and test data. Final evaluation uses a fixed test set that was not used for model selection, and retains per-class metrics and representative errors rather than only an average score.
Implementation sequence Define whether one prediction represents an image, a product, or an equipment time window. Keep raw data read-only and inspect file, label, equipment, Lot, and time metadata for missing or duplicate values. Fix train, validation, and test boundaries before training, considering equipment-, Lot-, or time-based groups. Fit preprocessing on training data only and establish a simple baseline. Train with recorded data version, split rule, model configuration, random seed, and runtime environment. Review per-class metrics and error cases under a fixed evaluation contract, then link the model, configuration, and report to the same run record. This sequence is a target standard for developing the repository; it is not a claim that every step is implemented and publicly verified.
Verified output and current stage The public repository currently supports only the stated direction of preprocessing, training, evaluation, and reproducibility management. It does not expose enough reproducible commands, dependency versions, dataset detail, or validated model results to support a quantitative achievement claim.
The present portfolio output is therefore an experiment-design standard, not a completed model. It also does not claim field validation on manufacturing data.
Deployment conditions and company value Manufacturing use requires separate validation: independent equipment-, Lot-, and time-based evaluation; condition-based slices for lighting or sensor variation; inference latency; out-of-distribution and failure behavior; and drift monitoring. Data rights, model version, decision threshold, approval, and rollback also need operating controls.
Under those conditions, a company could review where a model is trustworthy instead of relying on one score. Recording unsuccessful experiments in the same format can reduce repeated work and sharpen the next hypothesis. Any quality improvement or engineering-effort reduction still requires separate field evidence.

On the shop floor, the cost of missing a defect can matter more than aggregate accuracy, so the PoC separated data sources and prioritized recall and threshold decisions. Detection-criteria evaluation stage Period / basis Training team project · Public case updated Jul 2026 Project form Manufacturing DX PoC · Before production use Problem to solve A model that performs well on public data cannot be assumed to behave the same on field images with different lighting, angles, and surface conditions.
My scope Separated public training data from field practice images and ordered metric and threshold review around missed-defect risk. Verified result / current stage Verified output · Individual Public/field data separation and a recall- and threshold-led evaluation flow Current stage · Team Training PoC complete; not production-deployed Team boundary This was a training-team PoC; model results are not presented as production-quality performance.
Disclosure scope: Field images and company quality criteria are not disclosed; only the data separation and decision process are described.
The path from data collection to possible production use is generalized to the publicly shareable PoC scope.
Why the shop-floor decision mattered A missed micro-crack or pinhole can allow a defective weld to continue downstream. A false alarm creates reinspection work, but a missed defect can create a larger quality risk. In an imbalanced dataset, accuracy can remain high even when defects are missed, so the operating question was not simply how many images the model classified correctly. It was whether the model protected the defect class that the process could not afford to pass.
My battery-cell assembly experience with ultrasonic and laser welding informed that decision. The intended scope was a bounded inspection-assistance PoC that prioritizes candidates for human review, not a claim of completed autonomous inspection.
Why a digital method was needed Surface reflections and normal weld marks can resemble defects, while defect shapes are not uniform. A vision model was used because writing a complete set of fixed image rules would not cover that variation. The data sources were kept separate so that performance on public images would not be presented as field performance.
Approximately 60,000 AI-Hub public welding images supplied broad learning coverage. 198 field images provided a limited check under field capture conditions. They were not presented as one undifferentiated set of 60,198 training images. Camera, illumination, surface, and product conditions give each source a different purpose.
My actual role Within the team project, I worked on evaluation design and validation: F1, recall, false-positive behavior, model comparison, and threshold interpretation. The central tradeoff was to reduce false negatives first while deciding whether the remaining false positives could be handled through reinspection.
The team record progressed from a DenseNet-stage baseline through a two-model combination to a ResNet+DeiT ensemble. My contribution was to compare those stages within a common evaluation frame and interpret the operating threshold, not to present model complexity itself as the achievement.
Data flow Public-image learning base → model-stage comparison → limited field-image check → threshold search over probability outputs → confusion-matrix and error-image review → inspection-assistance rule
Keeping each prediction with its label and defect probability allowed precision, recall, and F1 to be compared across thresholds without retraining the model for every decision point.
Implementation sequence Align the meaning of public labels with the field defect definition. Separate the learning and field-check purposes and prevent overlap between training and evaluation. Compare the team’s recorded model stages with the same metrics. Review the mixed normal/defect region in the second test. Find threshold regions that retained 100% recall, then inspect precision and F1 within that region. Return false-positive and false-negative images to the next data, label, and capture-condition review. Verified output and current stage At the selected threshold on the recorded evaluation set, the report lists F1 93.10%, Recall 100%, and Precision 87.07%. Recall 100% means that no defect in that evaluation set was missed; it does not guarantee all future defects or all equipment conditions. Precision 87.07% shows that some predicted defects may be normal and require reinspection.
The current stage is a bounded PoC. The 198 field images do not cover every equipment, material, lighting, and product-shape condition, and the project is not presented as a production-line deployment.
Deployment conditions and company value Before deployment, the work needs independent product- or Lot-based splits, class-level sample review, standardized camera position and illumination, and latency and dropped-frame tests at line speed. Model version, threshold, image, equipment condition, and operator reinspection should be traceable, with approval and rollback for changes.
Under those conditions, the model could help inspectors review high-risk candidates first and feed recurring errors back into data improvement. The company value is a shared, auditable link between quality risk, model metrics, and reinspection policy. Any reduction in escaped defects or inspection time still requires controlled before-and-after measurement.

Debugging sequence and communication for the first time on physical equipment is expensive, so the project demonstrated why signal ownership and failure cases should be checked in a virtual environment first. Disclosure scope: Internal edit links and source material are not public; the case is limited to my role and the shareable system flow.
The flow below generalizes the team exercise for a virtual-commissioning context.
Why the shop-floor decision mattered With high-capital equipment, a sequence or communications problem discovered after installation is more expensive and riskier to correct. When sensor state, PLC logic, and operator displays disagree, the team also spends time deciding which information is authoritative. This project used a Giga Press factory context to examine how process and data connections could be checked before physical commissioning.
The scope was not a complete production Giga Press. It was a team PoC that connected Factory I/O, PLC, SCADA, and an upstream communications path to define what should be tested before moving to physical equipment.
Why a digital method was needed Testing only on physical equipment can reveal missing sensors, delayed completion signals, and restart conditions late in the project. A virtual process allows those abnormal cases to be repeated while the team checks whether control state and displayed data remain consistent.
The team kept control authority in the PLC. Factory I/O represented the virtual process, the PLC owned sequence and interlock decisions, SCADA displayed state and alarms, and the OPC UA path defined how upstream systems and an AI candidate could receive data. AI remained an optimization candidate rather than a safety controller.
My actual role This was a ten-person team project. My scope in the Digital Twin group was limited to AI-model selection and training, communications setup, and technical research. I reviewed a DQN candidate using realtime sensor and PLC data and organized where the OPC UA communications path fit within the team scenario.
Ladder and SCADA implementation belonged to other team members. They are described as parts of the team architecture, not as my individual work.
Data flow Field signals → PLC sequence and interlock decisions → Factory I/O virtual process and SCADA state display → OPC UA boundary → web and AI candidates
The layers see related signals but have different responsibilities. A displayed or AI-generated value does not become a safety command by itself; run permission and safe behavior during communications loss stay within PLC and dedicated safety design.
Implementation sequence The team defined the normal process sequence together with stop, delay, and restart conditions. The responsible team member connected Factory I/O scenarios to Ladder logic. The responsible team member configured SCADA state and alarm visibility. I selected and trained the AI candidate and handled communications setup and supporting research. The team integrated PLC, SCADA, Factory I/O, web, and AI-extension concepts into one demonstration and report. The report kept projected benefits separate from measured outcomes. Verified output and current stage The verified output is the team demonstration and report connecting process flow, Ladder and Factory I/O, SCADA, web, and an AI-extension structure. Validation with a production Giga Press safety PLC, hydraulic and servo dynamics, and real production I/O is outside the completed scope.
The report’s 50–75% setup-time reduction and 50% equipment-expansion labor reduction are expected benefits or targets for virtual commissioning and Ladder modularization. They are not controlled before-and-after plant results and are not presented as achievements.
Deployment conditions and company value Field use requires hardware-in-the-loop tests with actual I/O and safety requirements, communications-loss and reconnect tests, versioned tag specifications, alarm priorities, network segmentation, and access-control review. If an AI candidate is used, it cannot own run or safety commands; recommendations need approval, rejection, and rollback paths.
Under those conditions, virtual commissioning could move logic and data-integrity checks earlier than physical trial and give teams a reusable review standard. The company value is earlier change-impact review and accumulated commissioning knowledge. Time or labor savings can be confirmed only after measurement against a controlled baseline.

The same equipment or quality concept can be named differently across departments and documents, so terminology and relationships need an explicit contract before evidence-backed retrieval is possible. Disclosure scope: Only structures and code that can be checked in the public repository are described; local-only validation figures are excluded from achievements.
The case explains a general flow from manufacturing terminology contracts to retrieval.
Why the shop-floor decision mattered The same machine or defect can have different names across manufacturing documents. When process instructions, quality criteria, equipment history, and corrective-action records use inconsistent terminology, a search result does not establish that every document refers to the same subject. Unsupported explanations can also appear beside source-backed content.
HeungTology is a personal project for managing terminology and relationships under one contract and tracing a retrieved statement back to its source. The key decision was to separate “a document exists” from “this document supports this claim.”
Why a digital method was needed A person can navigate folders by memory only while the collection remains small. Consistent IDs, aliases, types, provenance, and relationships allow structural checks and support both exact-term and semantic retrieval.
Human-readable Markdown and YAML remain the authoring source. Graph and retrieval representations are derived from that source, preserving ownership and provenance while making relationships searchable.
My actual role As a personal project, I designed and implemented the YAML document contract, transformation and validation flow, knowledge-graph representation, and retrieval stages. Duplicate identities, missing relationship targets, local absolute paths, and format errors were defined as pre-release checks. Ambiguous relationships remain for human review rather than being attached automatically to the nearest-looking record.
For retrieval, vector and lexical raw scores are not added directly. Their candidate ranks are fused, and the final context carries its source path and heading so a reviewer can trace where the answer began.
Data flow Manufacturing terminology mismatch → YAML document contract → knowledge-graph representation → schema, relationship, and path validation → source-linked search use
YAML IDs and aliases let several terms resolve to one managed concept. Graph relationships support traversal across process, equipment, defect, cause, and action. Only validated material becomes a search candidate, and retrieved context includes its document and heading.
Implementation sequence Define a YAML contract for identity, title, aliases, type, lifecycle, provenance, and relationships. Separate conversion boundaries for graph representations used by JSON-LD, OWL, SHACL, and Neo4j. Validate schemas, identifiers, relationship targets, and local-path leakage; leave uncertain links for review. Build heading-aware retrieval data and fuse ranked lexical and vector candidates. Expand only selected relationships, rerank the context, and pass source path and heading with the answer material. Verified output and current stage The public repository supports claims about the data structure, transformation and validation code, and retrieval design documentation. Local release metrics or completion ratings that cannot be reproduced from public material are not used as achievements. This case does not claim node, assertion, error, or warning counts.
The current stage is a personal project demonstrating the structure and retrieval flow. The documents do not all have the same depth of human review, and retrieval quality still needs a fixed question set with relevance judgments.
Deployment conditions and company value Company use requires named terminology owners, controlled change and review procedures, provenance rules, access control, and audit history. Retrieval must remain read-only and separate from equipment control, so unsupported text cannot become an operating condition or work instruction.
Under those conditions, shared IDs and relationships could help teams find process conditions, equipment history, and corrective-action sources across departmental vocabulary. The company value lies in a reusable review and provenance structure, not in fluent search wording alone.

Disclosure scope: External repository links are withheld until internal network, local-path, and default-credential-shaped settings are removed.
The case is described as a generalized robot data flow separating control authority from observation.
Why the shop-floor decision mattered An Indy7 program is not only a list of positions. Tool and TCP settings, waypoints, motion commands, and the program tree reference one another. If a PC editor drops an unknown field or changes a reference, the file can look correct on screen and still fail on the teach pendant.
Communications ownership creates a related risk. If the HMI, historian, PLC integration, and digital twin each open a robot socket, it becomes difficult to trace command ownership and determine which state is current. Allowing display or storage features to create additional physical-control paths weakens the safety boundary.
Why a digital method was needed A PC-HMI makes hierarchical JSON easier to inspect and edit, but source compatibility must come before convenience. Unknown fields are therefore preserved, and the basic round-trip check is load → edit → save → reload → compare references.
For communications, one Robot Controller owns the IndyDCP connection. Other functions exchange command requests or consume state events. This keeps visualization and history from independently owning the physical-control socket.
My actual role In this project, I designed and prototyped the JSON compatibility layer, PC-HMI, Robot Controller-centered communications boundary, and the responsibilities of history and twin services. The design separates:
Command: the HMI sends a request with a command ID; only the Robot Controller executes IndyDCP commands. State and result: realtime robot state, connection, errors, and command outcomes are published as separate events. History: the DB Worker stores job, state, and error history without owning physical commands. PLC Bridge: PLC and HMI consumers exchange required state through an event contract; it is not an arbitrary bypass control path. Digital Twin: the twin is a read-only state consumer with no physical command controls. Data flow PC-HMI command request → Robot Controller’s single IndyDCP connection → command-result and realtime-state events → DB Worker history / PLC Bridge state exchange / read-only twin observation
Command, result, realtime state, connection, and error are not mixed into one message. A command ID connects each request to its outcome so the path remains traceable.
Implementation sequence Identify unknown Conty JSON fields and waypoint, program-tree, and motion-command references that must survive a round trip. Build the hierarchical JSON browser and editor around parser and serializer boundaries that preserve source data. Use an Offline UI stage to check file behavior and screen flow without a robot. Add a Direct stage in which the Robot Controller alone owns the IndyDCP connection. Add a Gateway stage that separates command, result, state, connection, and error events for the DB Worker, PLC Bridge, and twin consumers. Keep the twin read-only and omit physical command controls. Verified output and current stage The current output is a design and prototype joining JSON compatibility with PC-HMI and service ownership. It is not presented as production remote robot operation. Omniverse remains a future adapter direction rather than a completed integration.
The associated repository was reported to contain internal-network, local-path, and default-configuration patterns, so its external link remains withheld. Round-trip tests across Indy7 firmware versions and long-running reconnect and duplicate-command tests with hardware are still open.
Deployment conditions and company value Field connection requires firmware-specific JSON regression tests, command authentication and authorization, idempotency, MQTT topic permissions, timeout and reconnect behavior, and audit history. Hardware-in-the-loop testing must also confirm that the PLC Bridge and twin cannot bypass the Robot Controller’s single command boundary. Emergency stop and safety interlocks remain the responsibility of validated robot and PLC safety systems.
Under those conditions, the company could reduce the risk of corrupting program references and trace commands, state, and errors through one path. A read-only twin could share current state without creating a new control channel. Any reduction in downtime or editing effort still needs field measurement.
